content.text:
9 passing, all green. Now the refactor evaluation.

**Naming Evaluation (first priority)**

- `policyBasePremium` — the function now returns either a linear sum or a block price. Name still fits: it is "the base premium for the whole policy", regardless of how it is computed. Keep.
- `itemBasePremium`, `addPercent`, `roundPremium`, `quote`, `runStep` — all accurate. Keep.
- `COMPONENT_BLOCK_SIZE` / `COMPONENT_BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM` — accurate and domain-named.

One naming weakness: the literal `"rune"` inside the block check reads as "blocks are a rune thing", but the block rule is about *alike components*. The test that just passed only forces "3 runes", but the condition as written already says `items.every(item => item.type === "rune")`. Expressing "all items are the same type" instead of "all items are runes" is not implementing ahead — it is the same behaviour for every input the current tests cover, stated without an incidental hardcoded type. That said, it *would* change behaviour for 3 moonstones (currently 75, would become 60), which is untested. So that is generalisation, not refactoring. I'll leave the rune literal alone and just name it.

**APP mass, `policyBasePremium` before**

```
if                         conditional  4
items.length               binding      1
COMPONENT_BLOCK_SIZE       binding      1
items.every(...)           invocation   2
(item) => item.type        binding      1 + binding 1
"rune"                     constant     1
return COMPONENT_BLOCK_...  binding     1
items.reduce(...)          loop         5
total, item                bindings     2
itemBasePremium(item)      invocation   2
+                          invocation   2
0                          constant     1
```
Total: 24

**Rule 3 (duplication):** none — no repeated logic across functions.

**Rule 4 (fewest elements):** `itemBasePremium` is a one-line wrapper over a record lookup, invoked from exactly one place. Inlining it would drop an invocation (mass −2) and one function element. But it is the seam where unknown-type errors and per-item modifiers (curse, enchantment) will land, and it names the lookup. Rule 2 trumps mass here. Keep.

**Rule 2 (reveals intent):** the one real improvement available. The block condition is a bare boolean expression whose meaning ("this policy is a single block of three alike components") has to be reconstructed from `length ===` and `every`. Extracting a named predicate states the domain rule directly.

content.text: Still 9 passing. Let me also check the typecheck passes, since I changed a function body to an expression form.

Refactor phase complete. Tests stayed green throughout (9 passing, 42 todo), typecheck clean.

## What changed

One refactoring, applied to `/home/experimenter/experiments/runs/2026-09-14_17-35-07_claim-office-example-mapping_exact-hybrid-v2.4-lab-split-cc_opus-5-requesty-no-thinking-3/src/claim-office.ts`: split `policyBasePremium` into two named predicates/helpers plus a ternary that reads as the domain rule — `isComponentBlock(items) ? COMPONENT_BLOCK_BASE_PREMIUM : sumItemBasePremiums(items)`.

This is Rule 2 (reveals intent). The pricing decision is now one line that states the rule in domain words, and the two branches are each independently named. It is also the shape the later tests will need: `isComponentBlock` is exactly the predicate that has to grow when 4-runes and mixed-type cases arrive, and `sumItemBasePremiums` is the fallback that the grouping algorithm will call per-group.

## APP mass

`policyBasePremium` and its extractions: **24 → 28** (Δ +4). The extraction costs two invocations (+4) and duplicates the `items` parameter binding across three signatures, offset by dropping the `if`/`return` conditional structure into a ternary (both count as one conditional, so no change there).

Mass went **up**. I took that deliberately: Rule 2 trumps APP. Four points of mass buys a named statement of the block rule at the one place a reader looks to understand pricing, and the cost is entirely in function-call plumbing rather than in branching or mutation.

## What I deliberately did not do

- **Did not generalise the block rule.** The `items.every(item => item.type === "rune")` hardcodes `"rune"`, and writing "all items the same type" instead was tempting as a pure naming cleanup. It is not — it would change behaviour for 3 moonstones (75 today, 60 after), which no test covers. That is implementing ahead, so the rune literal stays until a test forces it. I left a comment marking it as test-limited.
- **Did not inline `itemBasePremium`.** It is a one-line, single-caller wrapper, so Rule 4 argues for removing it (−2 mass, one fewer element). But it is the seam where unknown-type errors and the per-item curse/enchantment surcharges will land, and it names the lookup. Kept.
- **Left the rounding and percentage helpers untouched** — `addPercent` keeps the integer-percent form and `roundPremium` keeps `Math.ceil`, as required. No payout path exists yet, so no `Math.floor` counterpart was added.
